How to calculate TRIR

TRIR (Total Recordable Incident Rate) is recordable cases times 200,000, divided by total hours worked. It answers one question: at this rate of recordable cases, how many would you expect per 100 full-time workers in a year? The rest of this page works through the formula on a real case count, not a rounded example.

The formula

TRIR = (recordable cases × 200,000) ÷ total hours worked

DART rate = (DART cases × 200,000) ÷ total hours worked

200,000 is OSHA's own base rate: 100 full-time employees, 40 hours a week, 50 weeks a year. It is fixed regardless of your company's actual headcount, which is what makes the rate comparable between a 12-person crew and a 400-person one.

Worked example

A contractor logs 6 OSHA-recordable cases over a year in which its employees worked 120,000 hours combined. 2 of those 6 cases involved days away, restricted duty, or a transfer (DART cases); the other 4 needed only medical treatment beyond first aid.

FigureArithmeticResult
TRIR6 × 200,000 ÷ 120,00010.00
DART rate2 × 200,000 ÷ 120,0003.33
Recordable, not DART6 − 24

Against a 3.0 target — a common GC prequalification ceiling — this contractor's TRIR of 10.00 is 7.00 points above target.

What it takes to close that gap

Holding the recordable count at 6 and adding no new case, the rate falls as more injury-free hours are worked: solve 6 × 200,000 ÷ target = hours needed for a target of 3.0, and subtract the 120,000 already worked. That is 400,000 − 120,000 = 280,000 additional injury-free hours — a real number a safety program can plan around, not a guess at how the rate might trend.

Do this with your own counts

The TRIR & DART rate calculator runs this same arithmetic on your own recordable count, DART count, and hours worked, lets you set whatever target rate a bid form or renewal is measuring you against, and converts the injury-free-hours figure into months if you give it your average monthly hours. Nothing you type leaves your browser.

Common questions

What is the TRIR formula?

TRIR = (number of OSHA-recordable cases × 200,000) ÷ total hours worked by all employees. 200,000 is OSHA's own base rate: the hours 100 full-time employees work in a year at 40 hours a week for 50 weeks, so the rate reads as recordable cases per 100 full-time workers per year regardless of a company's actual headcount.

What counts as a recordable case?

OSHA's recordkeeping rule (29 CFR 1904.7) defines it: a work-related injury or illness that results in death, days away from work, restricted work or transfer, medical treatment beyond first aid, loss of consciousness, or a significant diagnosed condition. Deciding whether a specific case meets that bar is the employer's own recordkeeping judgment call — this page and the calculator it links to start from a count you've already made, not from a case description.

Where do the case counts and hours worked come from?

Your own OSHA 300 Log of Work-Related Injuries and Illnesses, which every covered employer already keeps, and the OSHA 300A Summary posted every February. Total hours worked is the sum of hours actually worked by every employee in the period, including overtime, and excluding vacation, sick, and holiday time not actually worked.

No warranty. This page and the calculator it links to are arithmetic references, not legal, safety-compliance, insurance, or financial advice, and they do not determine whether any case is OSHA recordable or represent that any company is compliant with any OSHA rule. Verify every figure against your own OSHA 300 log and a qualified Certified Safety Professional before relying on it.       Common questions

      What is TRIR?

      TRIR (Total Recordable Incident Rate) is the number of OSHA-recordable injuries and illnesses per 100 full-time workers per year: recordable cases times 200,000, divided by total hours worked by all employees. 200,000 is OSHA's own base rate — the hours 100 full-time employees work in a year (40 hours a week, 50 weeks) — so the rate is comparable across companies of any size.

      What is DART rate?

      DART rate uses the same formula as TRIR but counts only cases involving Days Away from work, Restricted duty, or job Transfer — the recordable cases serious enough to keep someone from doing their normal job. It is always less than or equal to TRIR, because every DART case is also a recordable case, but not every recordable case is a DART case (a case needing only medical treatment beyond first aid is recordable but not DART).

      Does this tool decide whether an injury is OSHA recordable?

      No. Recordability is a judgment call made against OSHA's own recordkeeping rule (29 CFR 1904.7) — first aid vs. medical treatment, work-relatedness, and the general recording criteria — and it stays the employer's own determination, case by case. This tool starts from the counts already on your OSHA 300 log and does the rate arithmetic; it does not review, or reach a conclusion about, any individual case.

      Why does a GC prequalification form or insurance renewal ask for this?

      Many general contractors set a TRIR ceiling (often 3.0, or their trade's own published industry average) below which a subcontractor cannot bid, and workers' comp carriers use the same rate as one input to a renewal premium. A company that only calculates its rate once a year, when the OSHA 300A summary is due, is often seeing the number for the first time on the same form that is about to gate a bid or a renewal.

      How is the injury-free hours figure calculated?

      It holds your current recordable case count fixed and solves for how many more hours worked, with no new recordable case, would dilute the rate down to your target: recordable cases times 200,000, divided by the target rate, minus the hours already worked. It is not a prediction and it does not assume anything about future incidents — it is the arithmetic answer to 'if nothing else happens, how much more injury-free work does it take to reach that number.'

      Is my data uploaded anywhere?

      No account and no network requests — the calculator runs entirely in your browser. Nothing about your case counts, hours worked, or company is sent anywhere or stored anywhere but this device. The optional usage counter records only which features were used and the day, never any of your numbers.

      Is this a substitute for OSHA recordkeeping or a Certified Safety Professional?

      No. It is arithmetic on the counts you type in. It has no opinion on whether a specific case is recordable, does not review your OSHA 300 log for completeness, and is not a substitute for your own recordkeeping process, a Certified Safety Professional, or OSHA's own guidance. Verify every figure against your own log and a qualified professional before using it on a bid form or insurance submission.

vs-spreadsheet.html.text:
← back to the calculator

This calculator vs. a spreadsheet

A safety coordinator who reports TRIR more than once a year usually ends up with a spreadsheet for it: recordable cases times 200,000, divided by hours worked. That formula is correct the day it's built. It fails quietly later -- a DART formula copied from the TRIR cell without changing its range, or an hours-worked total nobody updated this quarter -- and neither failure looks wrong from the output alone.

What each one is for

A spreadsheet can compute TRIR and DART rate correctly, and most EHS teams already have one. What it does not do on its own is flag a copied formula pointing at the wrong case range, remind anyone to refresh the hours-worked total for the current period, or solve the reverse question of how many more injury-free hours close the gap to a target.

This calculator applies OSHA's own 200,000-hour formula (29 CFR 1904) fresh from the counts you enter every time, keeps TRIR and DART rate as two independently computed figures rather than one formula copied into a second cell, and adds the injury-free-hours-to-target figure -- the rearranged algebra a one-line spreadsheet formula stops short of.

QuestionWhere to answer it
Can I compute TRIR and DART rate in a spreadsheet?Yes -- if the formula is right and stays right as periods and case counts change.
Would I notice a DART formula silently pointing at the TRIR case range?Not from the output alone -- both cells would still show a plausible-looking rate.
Does either one remind me to refresh the hours-worked total for this period?Neither. Both trust whatever number is entered as this period's total hours.
Does either one tell me how many more injury-free hours reach a target rate?This calculator solves it directly. A spreadsheet only does if someone has already rearranged the formula for it.
Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere?No. The calculator runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent to a server.

Common questions

Can a spreadsheet calculate TRIR and DART rate correctly?

Yes -- the formula itself is one line: recordable cases times 200,000, divided by total hours worked. DART rate is the same formula against a different case count. Both are easy to get right once and easy to get wrong quietly later, which is where a hand-built sheet most often fails, not in the arithmetic itself.

What's the most common way a TRIR spreadsheet formula breaks?

The DART formula gets built by copying the TRIR formula and changing the multiplier reference, but not the case-count range -- so it silently reports the same number as TRIR, or a stale one, instead of the DART-only subset. A safety coordinator scanning the two output cells has no way to tell from the numbers alone that one of them is pointing at the wrong range.

Why does a stale hours-worked figure matter more than it looks like it would?

Because total hours worked is the denominator, and it is the one cell in the sheet with no natural trigger to update it. A recordable case gets entered the day it happens; hours worked for the quarter usually gets typed in once and left there. A rate computed against last quarter's hours total looks like a normal number -- it is just the wrong one.

Does a spreadsheet tell me how many injury-free hours it takes to hit a target rate?

Only if someone rearranges the formula for it, which almost none do. Solving for the hours that dilute a fixed case count down to a target rate means isolating hours worked on the other side of the TRIR equation -- an algebra step past the one-line formula most sheets stop at. Most safety coordinators who want that number instead guess at a timeline or wait for the annual OSHA 300A summary to see where the year landed.

Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere?

No. The calculator this page links to runs entirely in your browser; nothing you enter -- case counts, hours worked, or your company -- is uploaded or stored anywhere but this device.

No warranty. This page and the linked calculator apply OSHA's own TRIR and DART rate formulas (29 CFR 1904) to numbers you supply. It is not legal, safety-compliance, insurance, or financial advice, and it does not determine whether any case is OSHA recordable or represent that your company is compliant with any OSHA rule. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, and for checking it against your own OSHA 300 log and a qualified Certified Safety Professional.
